items.title: Code Safari: Go subcommands
items.author: John Arundel
items.content: DevOps engineer and mentor Gwyn James and I go on a low-key code safari into a Go package to see what we can find. No polish, no promotion, and absolutely no production values—or your money back.

items.title: The heat is on: handling units in Rust
items.author: John Arundel
items.content:
Hot enough for ya? Over the last few months, beginning with Here comes the sun, we’ve been building a little weather client in Rust, and it works pretty well:

It’s not just a command-line tool, of course: it’s also a crate that lets anyone write a Rust program to query the Weatherstack API and get weather data.

In Where the sun keeps shinin’, we created a “provider” abstraction that makes the crate more flexible and useful. So a minimal front end for this crate might look something like:

Since it’s the end of term, we’re allowed to bring in games. Let’s have a little fun now by implementing a bonus feature that should give my American friends a warm feeling: showing temperatures in Fahrenheit.

Converting from Celsius to Fahrenheit is straightforward, so shall we add an option that lets users request temperatures in Fahrenheit? See what you can do.

Adding a “Fahrenheit” feature

Make it so that users can get temperatures in Fahrenheit if they want.

It’s up to you how much engineering you want to do here. The least you could do is add a new flag to the program (, for example), and convert temperatures if the flag is supplied. On the other hand, you’re welcome to explore a deeper refactoring of the program if you like. We’ll talk over both approaches once you’ve had a go at this.

Throughout this series, and throughout my book The Secrets of Rust: Tools, we’ve emphasised the importance of doing the least possible work that solves the problem. It’s not that we should always stop there, of course; the point is just that if we to stop, we’d be in a reasonable place.

A ruthlessly minimal solution

So here’s about the least I can do:

We can’t do the conversion right here in , because the field isn’t public. Anyway, we don’t really want to do that, because, as we know, any code we write in is not importable. To really add a Fahrenheit feature to this program, we need to add it to the , which is why we invoke a new magic method on : .

We’ll say that takes a and returns a replacement whose temperature is expressed in Fahrenheit:

Fine. Not , but fine. So what’s unsatisfactory about this solution?

For one thing, it’s strange that is a method on , because Fahrenheit is a unit of , not weather. It’s also slightly annoying that, given a instance with unknown provenance, we don’t actually what units its temperature is in. Maybe it’s fresh from the API, in which case it’s Celsius, or maybe someone already called on it, in which case it isn’t.

And if we were to call again on a value that’s already been converted once, the result would just be wrong. Since we have no way of knowing what units a given is in, we can’t tell if it’s safe to call on it or not.

The real problem here is that temperature is not just a pure number, it’s a —that is, a measurement in some system of units. To unambiguously express a temperature, we need the units as well as the number. Rust’s built-in types don’t allow for that: expresses the numeric part, but it has no opinion about what units the user might have in mind.

So, while our current solution does work, after a fashion, it’s worth exploring what we’d do if we had the time to work on this a bit more. What do you think?

The “newtype” pattern and tuple structs

Well, it sounds as though we’re arguing that a conversion method, if we had one, should be on the value itself, rather than the containing struct. But the field is , and we can’t add methods willy-nilly to : it’s not our house to build an extension on.

A common trick in Rust when you want to add methods to somebody else’s type is to wrap it in your own type, like this:

Now we have a true quantity, because we can create a value of type , which an , but adds information to it: the type itself conveys the unit system.

We haven’t seen this kind of struct definition before, where we don’t give names to the fields, but Rust allows it: it’s called a . We’re defining and as structs with a single un-named field of type , which will hold the actual numeric value.

This way of wrapping an existing type is called the pattern, and it would indeed let us add methods to convert temperatures from one unit system to another. We could write, for example:

Making unit-agnostic

But this still doesn’t seem quite right. For one thing, which type should we declare for the field on ?

might seem to make sense, since that’s what the API gives us, but then if users want to convert that temperature to Fahrenheit, they can no longer store the result in a struct.

We’d like users to be able to deal with values regardless of temperature units. Indeed, we’d like to make values independent of a particular unit system. After all, the temperature is what it is, no matter what units you choose to express it in.

A struct with internal units

So what does that look like in Rust? Well, our intuition seems to be guiding us towards defining a type:

Again, we’re defining as a tuple (that is, list) of one element: an representing the temperature value. Since there’s only one field, it hardly needs a name, though you’re welcome to give it one if you like:

It comes to the same thing. The second version makes it clearer that the “internal” unit is Celsius, but we’re going to hide that from users altogether. We want them to be able to take some value in Celsius, and use it to create a unit-agnostic :

We also need to provide a way for them to express that temperature in their units of choice:

Notice that where we would ordinarily give a field name, with a tuple struct we give the field instead. And because the numbering starts from zero, and there’s only one field, then it must be field number 0:

If you prefer the “named field” version, you should replace this with .

Let’s check our conversions with a test, then:

We need to make a few tweaks to our existing code to cope with this change. For example:

By calling to create the , it’s clear right away that this temperature is in Celsius. (We could also have written a function, but we don’t need it for this program.)

Handle units and quantities with care

In general, whenever you deal with quantities in your Rust programs, it’s a good idea to use the type system like this to avoid potential confusion over units. We want to eliminate possible mistakes such as passing a distance in metres where a distance in feet was expected, or adding a force in pounds to a force in newtons. Rust gives us the tools to prevent disasters like that of the Mars Climate Orbiter, so let’s use them.

It’s also worth noting that quantities can have some subtle constraints and problems that aren’t always obvious. For example, our type is fine for expressing absolute temperatures, such as that experienced in London on a sunny day.

But it wouldn’t be suitable for expressing in temperature, such as saying that New York City is one Celsius degree warmer than the seasonal average. Converting that to Fahrenheit would give the wrong answer! So be careful, especially if your code needs to work on Mars (and you never know when someone might want to use it there).

Okay, so what about these temperatures? The version of we had before won’t work, because it assumes the temperature is Celsius:

But that’s sort of expected, because we’re that a given isn’t in any particular temperature units. It’s up to the user to choose these by giving the flag (or not), so let’s move this decision into the function:

Note that the temperature conversion is still part of our crate, where it can be imported and used in other programs. It’s only the to convert the temperature that lives in , where it arguably belongs—together with the choice about how to print it.

This means making the fields on public, but that’s okay: we’re only exposing the data, not the logic.

There’s more we could do here, but part of the skill of abstraction design is knowing when to stop—at least for now. While crate-oriented design is great, we should bear in mind that we’re here to write a general-purpose crate for every imaginable weather-related program. A good rule of thumb is to build just the functionality that we need for program, while not closing off any avenues for future expansion.

We’ve covered a lot of ground in this tutorial series, starting with Here comes the sun, and learned quite a few simple techniques for building and testing Rust API clients. That greatly expands the scope of tools we can write, because we can talk to any other program that exposes an HTTP interface.

If you’d like to learn more about writing practical programs in Rust, check out my book The Secrets of Rust: Tools: you’ll find dozens of code challenges to solve and working code samples to try. I hope you enjoy it!
